set1.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set1.q: What underlies xerosis, and who is most affected?
opts: Impaired stratum-corneum hydration promoted by ageing, low humidity, hot water, detergents, atopy and systemic disease, commonly affecting older adults especially in winter
Correct, causing tightness, pruritus, rough scale, fissuring or eczema.
Overgrowth of Malassezia in sebum-rich areas, in young men
That is seborrhoeic dermatitis.
Chronic venous hypertension in the lower legs, in older adults
That is stasis dermatitis.
An autoimmune process affecting the epithelial basement membrane, occurring most often in the elderly and remitting spontaneously after five or six years
That is bullous pemphigoid.

set1.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set1.q: Which nail changes are seen in psoriasis?
opts: Koilonychia and Beau's lines
Neither is the psoriatic pattern.
Terry's nails and clubbing
Neither is the psoriatic pattern.
Green nail discoloration and chronic paronychia of the nail folds
These indicate pseudomonas infection and soft tissue infection respectively.
Onycholysis, pitting, splinter haemorrhages and subungual hyperkeratosis
Correct — these can occur with any variant but are common in psoriatic arthritis.

set1.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set1.q: Why are the inguinal folds generally spared in irritant diaper dermatitis?
opts: They are less exposed to urine and faeces
Correct — the eruption follows exposure, so it lands on convex surfaces.
They have thicker skin than the surrounding area
Skin thickness is not the reason given.
They are protected by resident Candida
Candida is a complication rather than a protection.
They receive less friction from the diaper
Exposure to urine and faeces is the stated reason.

set1.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set1.q: Which adverse effects follow prolonged topical corticosteroid use?
opts: Hyperpigmentation and hypertrichosis
Hypopigmentation, not hyperpigmentation, is the listed effect.
Atrophy, striae, telangiectasia and hypopigmentation
Correct — which is why potency is matched to site and severity.
Photosensitivity, dryness and marked irritation
Those are the topical retinoid effects.
Nephrotoxicity and hepatotoxicity
Nephrotoxicity is a caution with calcipotriene rather than topical steroids.

set1.io: Objective a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
set1.q: How is a poorly demarcated lesion described?
opts: Present in more than one body region
That is distribution.
Raised above the surrounding skin surface
That is elevation, part of primary morphology.
Irregular or blotchy in appearance, without well-defined borders
Correct — as against a well demarcated lesion, which has clearly defined borders.
Smaller than one centimetre in every dimension measured
Demarcation is about border definition rather than size.

set1.io: Objective a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
set1.q: What does this lecture say about a patient presenting with purpura?
opts: It requires only outpatient dermatology follow-up
That understates the urgency stated.
It is diagnostic of thrombocytopenia
It raises concern but is not diagnostic of any single cause.
It is a medical emergency until proven otherwise
Correct — the lecture flags it explicitly rather than treating it as one finding among many.
It is a benign finding common in the elderly
The lecture treats it as an emergency until disproven.

set1.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set1.q: What does a Wood's lamp emit, and what is it used to evaluate?
opts: Infrared light, used to assess perfusion
This is not what a Wood's lamp does.
Short-wave ultraviolet light, used to sterilise the skin surface before a procedure is performed
It is a diagnostic device, not a sterilising one.
Long-wave ultraviolet light, used to evaluate pigment changes in selected fungal or bacterial infections
Correct — a handheld device highlighting subtle changes in skin, scalp and hair.
Polarised white light, used to magnify pigmented lesions
That describes a dermoscope.

set1.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set1.q: What is the mechanism of alopecia areata, and why is the hair loss non-permanent?
opts: Repeated traction pulls the follicle from the scalp
That is traction alopecia, not described here.
Autoreactive T cells infiltrate the follicle and switch it from growing to resting, without destroying the stem cell compartment
Correct — the stem cells survive, so regrowth remains possible.
Autoantibodies destroy the hair follicle and its entire stem cell compartment, so that any regrowth is never possible
The stem cell compartment is preserved.
Dihydrotestosterone progressively miniaturises the follicle
That is androgenetic alopecia.

set1.io: Objective a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
set1.q: What distinguishes a plaque from a patch?
opts: A plaque is always poorly demarcated while a patch is always well demarcated
Demarcation is described separately and varies for both.
A plaque is elevated and plateau-like; a patch is flat with no elevation
Correct — both exceed one centimetre, so elevation is the discriminator.
A plaque is larger than a patch
Both are greater than one centimetre; size does not separate them.
A plaque is fluid-filled and a patch is solid
Neither is fluid-filled.

set1.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set1.q: What is the central principle of managing lichen simplex chronicus?
opts: Systemic antibiotics given long term in order to prevent recurrent secondary infection
Infection is not the driver.
Excision of the affected plaque
Biopsy is reserved for atypical or treatment-resistant lesions rather than excision as treatment.
Break the itch-scratch cycle, since recurrence is common unless the initiating itch is controlled
Correct — through education, trigger treatment, emollients, behavioural substitution, nail care and safe occlusion.
Long-term high-potency topical steroids alone
A potent steroid is used for a limited course, not indefinitely as monotherapy.

set1.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set1.q: How does guttate psoriasis present, and what precedes it?
opts: Silvery plaques on the extensor elbows and knees
That is plaque psoriasis.
Erythematous patches with margins studded with subcorneal pustules, appearing typically during the third trimester of pregnancy
That is impetigo herpetiformis, psoriasis of pregnancy.
Raindrop-shaped erythematous papules and plaques in children, typically 2 to 3 weeks after a streptococcal infection or upper respiratory infection
Correct. It often needs no treatment, though phototherapy and topical steroids may be used.
Sudden generalised pustules with fever over the trunk and extremities
That is pustular psoriasis, the Von Zumbusch form.

set1.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set1.q: Where do pemphigus vulgaris lesions typically begin, and in which populations is it more common?
opts: On the lower legs in the gaiter region, and it is far more common in older men than women
That distribution fits stasis dermatitis.
On the scalp, and it is more common in children
Pemphigus is a disease of adults and begins in the mouth.
In the axillae, and it is endemic in rural Brazil
Endemic rural Brazil describes pemphigus foliaceus.
In the mouth, and it is more common in Jewish populations and people of Mediterranean descent
Correct. Pemphigus foliaceus by contrast is endemic in rural Brazil and rarely involves mucosa.

set1.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set1.q: Why does the medication history ask when each drug was started in relation to the rash?
opts: Because the timing between starting a drug and the eruption is what implicates it
Correct — a new rash after starting a medication, especially with fever or mucosal sores, is an urgent warning sign.
Because most drug eruptions occur only after six months of continuous therapy
No such interval is given.
Because only prescription medications can cause eruptions
Antibiotics, pain relievers, supplements, vitamins and herbal products are all asked about.
Because the dose determines whether a reaction is possible
Timing rather than dose is what the history targets.

set1.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set1.q: Which genetic marker is seen in 90% of early-onset psoriasis?
opts: HLA-B27
That is frequently associated with psoriatic arthritis.
PSORS1
That is the major susceptibility locus rather than the 90% marker.
HLA-DR4
This marker is not named in the lecture.
HLA-Cw6
Correct, and in 50% of late-onset cases. PSORS1 is the major susceptibility locus; HLA-B27 associates with psoriatic arthritis.

set1.io: Objective a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
set1.q: What distinguishes a pustule from a vesicle?
opts: A pustule contains leukocytes; a vesicle contains clear fluid
Correct — the contents, not the size, separate them.
A pustule is larger than one centimetre and a vesicle is smaller
That is the vesicle-to-bulla distinction.
A pustule is solid and a vesicle is fluid-filled
Both contain fluid.
A pustule sits in the dermis and a vesicle in the epidermis
Depth is not what distinguishes them here.

set1.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set1.q: What are the four Ps of lichen planus?
opts: Painful, pale, punched-out papules
That is not the mnemonic.
Pruritic, pustular, patchy plaques
That is not the mnemonic.
Purple, painless, peripheral pustular lesions
That is not the mnemonic.
Pruritic, purple, polygonal, papules or plaques
Correct — flat-topped, pink to violaceous and shiny, coalescing into larger plaques.

set1.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set1.q: Which patients with lichen planus are at increased risk of squamous cell carcinoma?
opts: Those with cutaneous disease of the wrists and ankles only
The increased risk is stated for genital and erosive oral disease.
Those with nail involvement
Nail involvement occurs but is not the stated risk.
Those with hepatitis C
Hepatitis C may associate with incidence, but the malignancy risk is stated for genital and erosive oral disease.
Those with genital and erosive oral disease
Correct — an important reason to identify and follow mucosal involvement.

set1.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set1.q: Which treatment is contraindicated in pregnancy for pustular psoriasis, and what is used instead?
opts: Phototherapy is contraindicated in pregnancy; acitretin is used instead
The contraindication given is for acitretin.
Biologics are first line in pregnancy
That is not what the lecture specifies.
Acitretin is contraindicated; high-potency topical steroids are used if pregnant
Correct.
Methotrexate is safe in pregnancy and is preferred
Methotrexate is not the safe option in pregnancy.

set1.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set1.q: What is the main differential for nummular eczema, and what distinguishes them?
opts: Tinea corporis — tinea has central clearing and nummular eczema does not
Correct, and this single feature is the discriminator the lecture gives.
Psoriasis — psoriasis has silvery scale and nummular eczema does not
Psoriasis is a differential for other conditions but is not the one named here.
Pityriasis rosea — pityriasis has a herald patch
Pityriasis rosea is not the named main differential.
Contact dermatitis — contact dermatitis is well demarcated
Contact dermatitis is not the named main differential.

set1.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set1.q: How does eczema change in appearance from acute to chronic?
opts: Acute shows pigment loss; chronic shows vesiculation
Neither is correct for the stage described.
Acute shows erythema, oedema, papules, vesicles, oozing and crusting; chronic shows xerosis, fissuring, lichenification and pigment alteration
Correct, with a subacute stage of scaling, erythema, papules and excoriations between them.
Acute disease shows lichenification and pigment alteration; chronic disease shows erythema, oedema, vesicles, oozing and crusting
The stages are reversed.
The appearance is fixed and does not evolve over time
Eczema changes appearance over time, which is the point being made.

set1.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set1.q: What is finasteride, and what are its cautions?
opts: A topical 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor applied to the crown, whose effects on libido and erectile function are permanent and do not reverse at all when the drug is stopped
The effects are reversible when the drug is stopped.
An oral 5-alpha-reductase type 2 inhibitor; about 2% of men report reduced libido and erectile function, reversible on stopping, and it is not indicated in women and contraindicated in pregnancy
Correct, and it works best combined with minoxidil.
A topical vasodilator effective mainly at the crown
That describes minoxidil.
An oral antiandrogen used first line in women
Finasteride is not indicated in women; oral antiandrogens such as combined oral contraceptives may be considered instead.

set1.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set1.q: How do urushiol lesions present, and over what time course?
opts: Well-demarcated plaques shaped like the object contacted, erupting within minutes of exposure and clearing within a day
That pattern fits metal, adhesive or jewellery allergy rather than urushiol.
Diffuse urticarial wheals resolving within 24 hours
That describes urticaria.
Greasy scaling patches in sebum-rich areas over several weeks
That describes seborrhoeic dermatitis.
Intensely pruritic vesicular lesions in linear distributions, erupting within 4 to 96 hours and persisting up to 3 weeks
Correct — the linear pattern comes from grazing the plant in passing.

set1.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set1.q: How does plaque psoriasis classically present?
opts: Poorly demarcated plaques in the flexures
That is atopic dermatitis.
Erythematous to salmon pink papules and plaques with silvery scale on extensor elbows and knees, trunk, scalp, umbilicus, sacrum, and the tip of the penis and scrotum
Correct, with Koebner's phenomenon and the Auspitz sign.
Greasy yellow scaling in sebum-rich areas
That is seborrhoeic dermatitis.
Coin-shaped, intensely pruritic light pink scaly plaques scattered over the extremities and the trunk, uniform in appearance and without any degree of central clearing
That is nummular eczema.

set1.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set1.q: What is the atopic triad, and what proportion of patients have at least one of its components?
opts: Asthma, allergic rhinitis and chronic sinusitis — approximately 60%
Atopic dermatitis is part of the triad by definition.
Atopic dermatitis, asthma and allergic rhinitis — approximately 80%
Correct.
Atopic dermatitis, urticaria and food allergy — approximately 50%
Urticaria and food allergy are not the named triad.
Eczema, psoriasis and seborrhoeic dermatitis — approximately 30%
These are separate conditions rather than a triad.

set1.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set1.q: How is mild perioral dermatitis treated once the corticosteroid is stopped?
opts: A higher-potency topical corticosteroid applied twice daily
Continued corticosteroid exposure perpetuates the condition.
Topical ketoconazole
Antifungals are the mainstay of seborrhoeic dermatitis rather than this.
Oral prednisone
Systemic steroids are not the treatment described.
Topical metronidazole, erythromycin, pimecrolimus or azelaic acid
Correct, with oral tetracycline or doxycycline for more extensive or persistent disease.

set1.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set1.q: How does the distribution of atopic dermatitis change with age?
opts: The distribution is the same at every age
Distribution evolves with age, which the lecture stresses.
Infants: palms and soles. Children: trunk. Adults: lower legs
None of these matches the described pattern.
Infants: cheeks, scalp and extensor surfaces. Children: antecubital and popliteal fossae, wrists and ankles. Adults: flexures, hands, neck, face and eyelids
Correct — the shift from extensor to flexural is the pattern to hold.
Infants: flexures and popliteal fossae. Children: extensor surfaces and scalp. Adults: cheeks, scalp and the extensor surfaces of the limbs
The infantile and childhood patterns are reversed.

set1.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set1.q: Which biopsy takes the whole lesion with deep and wide margins?
opts: Excisional biopsy
Correct, and it always needs stitches to close.
Punch biopsy
A punch biopsy samples deeply but does not take the whole lesion with margins.
Shave biopsy
A shave biopsy removes only surface skin.
Incisional biopsy
This is not one of the three described in the lecture.

set1.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set1.q: How does the timing of irritant contact dermatitis vary with the irritant?
opts: Timing does not vary with the irritant
The lecture states it varies by exposure.
Mild irritants such as soaps may progress over weeks, while alkalis and acids may present within minutes or be delayed up to 24 hours or more
Correct — the agent determines the tempo.
All irritants produce symptoms within minutes of exposure
Mild irritants can take weeks.
All irritants produce symptoms 48 to 72 hours after exposure regardless of whether the agent is a mild soap or a concentrated acid
That timing belongs to delayed hypersensitivity in the allergic form.

set1.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set1.q: What underlies stasis dermatitis?
opts: Chronic venous hypertension, most commonly from chronic venous insufficiency
Correct — incompetent valves, obstruction or impaired calf-muscle pumping raise venous pressure.
Arterial insufficiency arising from established peripheral arterial disease
Arterial disease is a differential and a safety consideration, not the cause.
Lymphatic obstruction
Lymphoedema is listed among the differentials rather than the cause.
Autoimmune damage to the basement membrane
That is bullous pemphigoid.

set1.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set1.q: What pattern does the pityriasis rosea eruption follow, and over what course?
opts: It follows cleavage lines on the trunk in a Christmas tree pattern, spreading top down over days and fading over 4 to 6 weeks
Correct. The herald patch clears centrally leaving a cigarette-paper or collarette of scale.
It follows a dermatome and resolves within two weeks
That describes shingles.
It follows flexural creases and persists for months
That is not the described pattern.
It appears on the extensor surfaces of the limbs and persists indefinitely unless it is treated with phototherapy
That is closer to psoriasis.

set2.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set2.q: What is the relationship between the terms dermatitis and eczema?
opts: Dermatitis is infectious and eczema is inflammatory
Dermatitis refers to inflammatory disorders, not infectious ones.
Dermatitis is a broad term for inflammatory skin disorders; eczema describes a pruritic inflammatory reaction pattern, and the two are used interchangeably
Correct. Atopic dermatitis is the commonest eczema, which is why 'eczema' often means it.
Eczema is the broad category for inflammatory skin disorders and dermatitis is one pruritic subtype within it, so the two should never be used interchangeably
The hierarchy runs the other way.
They describe the same condition at different ages
Neither term is age-defined.

set2.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set2.q: Nail clipping with periodic acid-Schiff stain evaluates which suspected condition?
opts: Alopecia areata
Nail pitting occurs in alopecia areata, but this test is not how it is assessed.
Onychomycosis
Correct.
Psoriatic nail disease
Nail changes occur in psoriasis but this stain targets fungal infection.
Subungual melanoma
That would require biopsy of the nail matrix.

set2.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set2.q: What is the usual application schedule for topical corticosteroids given in this lecture?
opts: Twice a day indefinitely for chronic conditions
Prolonged use risks atrophy, striae, telangiectasia and hypopigmentation.
Twice a day for two weeks
Correct, with potency selected according to site and severity.
Once a day for six weeks
That is not the schedule given.
Three times a day until the rash resolves
That is not the schedule given.

set2.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set2.q: How do seborrhoeic dermatitis lesions appear, and where?
opts: Well-demarcated salmon plaques with prominent silvery scale on the extensor elbows, knees, trunk, scalp, umbilicus and sacrum
That describes plaque psoriasis.
Coin-shaped plaques without central clearing on the extremities
That describes nummular eczema.
Tense bullae on the trunk and flexures
That describes bullous pemphigoid.
Poorly demarcated pruritic erythematous plaques 5 to 20 mm, greasy with flaking or yellow scaling, in areas rich in sebaceous glands
Correct — scalp, eyebrows, under facial hair, nasolabial creases, forehead, nose, behind the ears and the external auditory canal.

set2.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set2.q: How are severe or extensive allergic contact dermatitis eruptions treated?
opts: High-dose oral corticosteroids tapered over two to three weeks, because early discontinuation causes high rates of rebound
Correct. Limited eruptions can be managed with high-potency topical steroids.
High-potency topical steroids alone regardless of how extensive the eruption is across the body surface area
Topical therapy suits limited body surface area only.
A five-day course of oral corticosteroids without taper
Early discontinuation results in high rates of rebounding.
Oral antihistamines alone
Antihistamines address itch but are not the treatment for severe eruptions.

set2.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set2.q: A mineral oil preparation is used to confirm which diagnosis?
opts: Bullous pemphigoid, by identifying basement membrane antibodies
That uses direct immunofluorescence or serum studies.
Allergic contact dermatitis, by identifying the causative allergen
That uses patch testing.
Scabies infestation, by identifying the mite, its eggs or its faecal pellets
Correct — a rapid bedside test.
Onychomycosis, by identifying fungal elements in the nail
That uses nail clipping with periodic acid-Schiff stain.

set2.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set2.q: Who most commonly develops nummular eczema?
opts: Infants and young children
That pattern fits atopic dermatitis rather than nummular eczema.
Adolescents in the weeks following a streptococcal throat infection
That pattern fits guttate psoriasis.
Men, and more often adults over the age of 50, though it can occur at any age
Correct. It is likely caused by some degree of skin barrier dysfunction.
Women in their twenties and thirties
It is more common in men and in older adults.

set2.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set2.q: What is first-line treatment for alopecia areata by age group?
opts: Systemic corticosteroids in all age groups
Intralesional and topical routes are specified rather than systemic.
Intralesional steroids in adolescents and adults; topical steroids in children aged ten and under
Correct, and psychological support is named as one of the most important considerations.
Topical minoxidil at every age
Minoxidil is used for androgenetic alopecia.
Oral finasteride in adults and topical minoxidil in children under the age of ten years
Finasteride is for male-pattern hair loss.

set2.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set2.q: Which finding should raise concern for deep venous thrombosis in a patient with suspected stasis dermatitis?
opts: Atrophie blanche
That is a chronic feature of stasis disease.
Acute unilateral swelling or pain
Correct. Other considerations include peripheral arterial disease, vasculitis, lymphoedema and cutaneous malignancy.
Bilateral chronic hyperpigmentation
That is the expected chronic picture of stasis dermatitis itself.
Pruritus with scaling
That fits the dermatitis rather than a thrombosis.

set2.io: Objective a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
set2.q: What distinguishes an ulceration from an erosion?
opts: An ulceration is full-thickness loss extending to the dermis or deeper; an erosion loses only the epidermis
Correct — depth is the discriminator, and it determines whether the lesion can scar.
An ulceration is linear and an erosion is round
Shape does not distinguish them.
An ulceration is painful and an erosion is painless
Neither is defined by pain.
An ulceration involves only the epidermis and always heals without scarring, while an erosion reaches the dermis or deeper
The definitions are reversed.

set2.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set2.q: At what level does blistering occur in bullous pemphigoid, and who does it affect?
opts: Intraepithelial, from Malassezia overgrowth, in middle-aged men
That organism causes seborrhoeic dermatitis.
Subepithelial, from autoimmune damage to the epithelial basement membrane, twice as often in men, typically after age 60
Correct — a relatively benign disease usually remitting in five to six years.
Intraepithelial, from loss of keratinocyte adhesion, in young adults
That describes pemphigus.
Subepithelial, from a delayed type IV hypersensitivity reaction, most often in children and young adults
The mechanism is autoimmune damage to the basement membrane, not hypersensitivity.

set2.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set2.q: What causes irritant contact dermatitis, and how common is it relative to the allergic form?
opts: An immunoglobulin E-mediated immediate hypersensitivity reaction, and it is the most common form of contact dermatitis
Irritant contact dermatitis is not immunologically mediated.
Overgrowth of Malassezia, and it is the most common form
That is seborrhoeic dermatitis.
A response to chemicals or friction that disrupts the skin barrier, and it is the most common form of contact dermatitis
Correct — frequently occupational, as in healthcare and janitorial staff who wash their hands often.
A delayed type IV hypersensitivity reaction, and it is the less common form
That describes allergic contact dermatitis.

set2.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set2.q: How is pityriasis rosea treated?
opts: It is self-limited, so reassurance is the mainstay, with antihistamines or topical steroids used cautiously for pruritus
Correct. Ultraviolet B phototherapy or sunlight helps if begun in the first week; severe cases may be treated with acyclovir.
A tapering course of oral prednisone given over a period of two to three weeks from the outset of the eruption
That is used for severe allergic contact dermatitis.
Topical ketoconazole
That treats seborrhoeic dermatitis.
Oral doxycycline for six weeks
That is not the treatment for this condition.

set2.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set2.q: What is the Auspitz sign?
opts: Lesions appear at sites of trauma
That is the Koebner phenomenon.
The top layers of skin slough when rubbed
That is the Nikolsky sign.
Fine white lines on the surface of a plaque
Those are Wickham's striae.
Removal of scale produces bleeding
Correct — a classic psoriasis finding, alongside Koebner's phenomenon.

set2.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set2.q: How are nummular eczema plaques described?
opts: Intensely pruritic, round coin-shaped, light pink, scaly, thin plaques 1 to 10 cm, uniform without central clearing
Correct, most commonly on the extremities though they can occur on the trunk.
Well-demarcated salmon-pink plaques with prominent silvery scale on the extensor surfaces of the elbows and knees
That describes plaque psoriasis.
Greasy yellow scaling plaques in sebum-rich areas
That describes seborrhoeic dermatitis.
Violaceous flat-topped polygonal papules with fine white lines
That describes lichen planus.

set2.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set2.q: How do male- and female-pattern hair loss differ in distribution?
opts: Male pattern recedes at the frontotemporal hairline in a triangular pattern then the vertex; female pattern thins diffusely in central and parietal regions without significant frontal hairline change
Correct — preservation of the frontal hairline is the female-pattern hallmark.
Both begin at the vertex and spread forward
Only the male pattern involves the vertex in that way.
Male pattern produces diffuse thinning of the central and parietal scalp while female pattern recedes at the frontotemporal hairline in a triangular shape then the vertex
The patterns are reversed.
Both produce discrete round patches
Round patches describe alopecia areata.

set2.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set2.q: What is the mechanism of pemphigus?
opts: Loss of keratinocyte-to-keratinocyte adhesion, called acantholysis, from autoantibodies to adhesion molecules, producing intraepithelial blisters
Correct — a life-threatening blistering disorder of skin and mucous membranes.
Autoimmune damage to the epithelial basement membrane producing subepithelial blistering that resolves without any scarring
That is bullous pemphigoid.
A type IV delayed hypersensitivity reaction to an external allergen
That is allergic contact dermatitis.
Impaired stratum-corneum hydration
That is xerosis.

set2.io: Objective a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
set2.q: What is lichenification?
opts: A break in the skin
That is a fissure.
Abnormal formation of connective tissue
That is a scar.
Thickening and hardening of the skin
Correct — it develops from chronic rubbing or scratching.
Accumulation of loose cornified fragments of the epidermis
That is scaling.

set2.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set2.q: What proportion of children worldwide are affected by atopic dermatitis, and in which sex is it more common?
opts: About 20% of children, more common in females
It is more common in males.
About 5% of children, more common in males
The figure given is 20%.
About 40% of children, with no sex difference
Neither figure nor the absence of a sex difference matches.
About 20% of children, more common in males
Correct. It often begins in infancy or childhood; adult-onset disease occurs but is rare.

set2.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set2.q: What is the foundation of treatment for diaper dermatitis?
opts: Oral antibiotics to prevent secondary infection
Antibiotics are used only when bacterial infection is clinically supported.
A high-potency topical corticosteroid until resolution
Only a brief course of a low-potency steroid is used, under guidance.
Reducing moisture and irritant exposure through frequent changes, gentle cleansing, air exposure and superabsorbent diapers, with a thick zinc oxide or petrolatum barrier at each change
Correct. The previous barrier layer need not be scrubbed away if it remains clean.
A topical antifungal applied at every diaper change regardless of cause, together with a course of oral antibiotics to prevent secondary bacterial infection of the damaged barrier
Antifungals are added when candidal disease is suspected or confirmed.

set2.io: Objective a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
set2.q: Which six features are used to translate a dermatological finding into words?
opts: Primary morphology, secondary morphology, demarcation, colour, size and distribution
Correct. Getting all six into a description is what lets another provider picture the lesion without seeing it.
Primary morphology, colour and distribution only, since the rest are subjective
Demarcation, secondary morphology and size are all part of the description.
Onset, duration, severity, triggers, treatments tried and response
Those come from the history rather than the description of the lesion.
Location, laterality, symmetry, tenderness, temperature and texture
These are not the six features named.

set2.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set2.q: Which finding is pathognomonic for alopecia areata?
opts: Diffuse thinning of the central scalp
That is female-pattern hair loss.
Receding frontotemporal hairline
That is male-pattern hair loss.
Exclamation point hairs
Correct — thinner at the root and normal calibre at the top, because growth is changing in real time.
Broken hairs close to the scalp with scaling
That is tinea capitis.

set2.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set2.q: What is first-line treatment for dyshidrotic eczema?
opts: High-potency topical corticosteroids
Correct, with systemic corticosteroids reserved for severe cases.
Low-potency topical corticosteroids
High potency is specified as first line for this condition.
Topical antifungals
The condition is not fungal; its aetiology is unknown.
Oral antibiotics
Antibiotics are not first-line here.

set2.io: Objective a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
set2.q: What defines a wheal?
opts: A fluid-filled lesion containing leukocytes
That is a pustule.
A fluid-filled lesion under one centimetre
That is a vesicle.
A deposit of blood in the skin measuring one to two millimetres across
That is a petechia.
A firm oedematous plaque produced by infiltration of fluid into the dermis
Correct — the fluid is in the tissue rather than in a cavity, which is what separates it from a vesicle.

set2.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set2.q: What are Wickham's striae?
opts: Silvery scale on psoriatic plaques
That is the scale of plaque psoriasis.
Linear excoriations from scratching
Those are excoriations rather than striae.
Atrophic stretch marks from prolonged topical steroid use
Those are striae from steroid atrophy, a different finding.
Fine white lines visible on the surface of lichen planus plaques
Correct. On the buccal mucosa oral lichen planus appears as lacey white lesions.

set2.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set2.q: When should herpes simplex virus polymerase chain reaction be ordered in atopic dermatitis?
opts: Only when the patient has known herpes simplex
The test is used to establish it, not confirm a known case.
Only in adult-onset disease
The trigger is the lesion morphology, not the age of onset.
For painful monomorphic erosions or systemic illness
Correct. Culture is reserved instead for purulent, pustular or significantly crusted lesions.
For every flare, since secondary infection is common
It is targeted to that specific presentation rather than routine.

set2.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set2.q: How is pemphigus initially treated?
opts: With ultrapotent topical steroids alone
Those are used for mild bullous pemphigoid rather than pemphigus.
With watchful observation alone, since the disease usually remits spontaneously within five to six years without treatment
Spontaneous remission over five to six years describes bullous pemphigoid.
With oral doxycycline as monotherapy
Doxycycline is an option in moderate bullous pemphigoid, not pemphigus.
Urgently, with rituximab or high-dose oral prednisone, often alongside azathioprine or mycophenolate so steroids can be tapered off
Correct. It is a life-threatening disorder, so treatment is urgent.

set2.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set2.q: Which medications can produce lichenoid reactions?
opts: Topical corticosteroids
Those are associated with perioral dermatitis rather than lichenoid reactions.
Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, sulfonamides, tetracyclines, hydrochlorothiazide, quinidine and some beta blockers
Correct — worth asking about, since the eruption can mimic idiopathic lichen planus.
Penicillins, cephalosporins and the macrolide antibiotics, taken either together as a class or individually
These are not the named agents.
Statins and proton pump inhibitors
These are not the named agents.

set2.io: Objective a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
set2.q: How are petechiae and purpura distinguished by size in this lecture?
opts: Petechiae are under 3 mm and purpura are 3 mm to 1 cm
That is the Clinical Pathophysiology convention rather than this lecture's.
Petechiae are 4 mm or greater and purpura are 1 to 2 mm, the reverse of the usual
The sizes are reversed.
Both are defined as deposits of blood greater than 1 cm
Neither is defined that way; over 1 cm would be an ecchymosis.
Petechiae are deposits of blood 1 to 2 mm; purpura are 4 mm or greater
Correct, and purpura is flagged as a medical emergency until proven otherwise.

set2.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set2.q: Which biopsy technique cuts deep into the fat layers and is preferred for rashes or deeper bumps?
opts: Curettage
This technique is not among the three described.
Punch biopsy
Correct — it often needs one or two stitches.
Shave biopsy
A shave biopsy takes surface skin only and needs no stitches; it suits moles and growths on top.
Excisional biopsy
An excisional biopsy removes the whole lesion with deep and wide margins and always needs stitches.
